summary: MISSION MOHAKASH is a 3D chibi-style space survival and exploration game built with Unity for mobile and desktop, designed to make space science engaging for children aged 7–12. Players control a single astronaut across 6 unique missions on the Moon and Mars, completing objectives while managing oxygen, power, food, health, radiation, and fatigue. Through interactive habitats, rover exploration, resource management, and environmental hazards, players experience the real challenges of sustaining an extraterrestrial outpost. The game incorporates NASA resources, including DONKI, Moon Trek, and Mars Trek, to connect gameplay with real space weather events and planetary geography.

MISSION MOHAKASH

Explore. Survive. Discover.

1. Project Overview

MISSION MOHAKASH is a 3D chibi-style space survival, exploration, and resource-management game developed using Unity. It is designed to make the challenges of human space exploration understandable and exciting for children aged 7–12.

The game places players in control of a single astronaut responsible for operating and maintaining an extraterrestrial outpost. Players must prepare for missions, manage limited resources, maintain life-support systems, explore unfamiliar planetary environments, and complete scientific objectives while keeping the astronaut alive.

Our project focuses on demonstrating that surviving in space requires more than reaching another planet. It requires careful planning, scientific knowledge, resource management, and difficult decisions.

3. What Does the Game Do?

MISSION MOHAKASH features six missions across two planetary environments: the Moon and Mars.

The six missions are:

  1. First Flight (Moon): A beginner-friendly tutorial that introduces astronaut controls, habitat systems, and basic survival mechanics.
  2. Start the Outpost (Moon): Establish the outpost, deploy a seismometer at a designated location away from the habitat, and survive while completing the objective.
  3. Sample Collection (Moon): Travel to a specific geological location and collect rock samples using drilling equipment.
  4. Lunar Survival (Moon): Maintain the outpost and survive for a specified number of days while managing limited resources.
  5. Mars Exploration (Mars): Produce oxygen from the Martian atmosphere and collect rock samples from a distant location.
  6. Dust Storm Survival (Mars): Survive a Martian dust storm, manage reduced solar power generation, and repair and clean affected equipment.

Each mission introduces different objectives, environmental conditions, and resource-management challenges.

4. How Does It Work?

Mission Preparation

Before launching a mission, players receive a limited amount of Mission Credits (MC). They must strategically select additional equipment and supplies, such as food, oxygen tanks, solar panels, and repair equipment. Some essential supplies are provided automatically.

This system teaches players that mission preparation requires prioritization because carrying additional resources has a cost.

Astronaut Survival System

Players control one astronaut and monitor five primary status attributes:

  • Health Points (HP): Represents the astronaut's physical condition.
  • Radiation Dose: Tracks accumulated radiation exposure.
  • Hunger: Represents the astronaut's need for food.
  • Thrust Points: Represents the available movement or propulsion resource in the game.
  • Fatigue: Tracks physical exhaustion and the need for rest.

Players must maintain these attributes throughout the mission.

Habitat and Life-Support Systems

The habitat is the astronaut's primary living and operational facility. It contains interconnected systems and modules, including:

  • Oxygen storage and life-support systems.
  • Electrical power storage and management.
  • Bed for fatigue recovery.
  • Bathroom facilities.
  • Oxygen refilling station for spacesuits.
  • Communication desk for contacting Earth and requesting resources.
  • Storage facilities for mission equipment and supplies.

Solar panels generate electricity when exposed to sunlight, and the generated energy is stored in the habitat's power system. Oxygen reserves supply the astronaut's breathing requirements.

Spacesuit and Exploration

When leaving the habitat, the astronaut must use a spacesuit with a limited oxygen supply. The suit can be refilled using the habitat's oxygen refilling station or an available external oxygen storage tank.

Players must carefully plan their outside activities and return before their life-support reserves become dangerously low.

Rover Exploration

The game includes two types of rovers:

  • Remote-Controlled Mini Rover: Controlled from inside the habitat to explore nearby areas without requiring the astronaut to leave the base. It has its own battery, an external charging station, and a small solar panel for slow energy generation.
  • Crew-Driven Rover: A larger vehicle stored in a dedicated garage. The astronaut can drive it to explore distant locations and complete exploration objectives. It receives energy from the habitat's power storage system.

Earth Communication

The communication desk allows the astronaut to send reports, receive mission instructions, and request additional supplies from Earth.

Communication takes time, and resource requests require waiting for delivery. This introduces players to the communication delays and logistical difficulties associated with operating distant space missions.

5. Environmental Hazards

The game includes environmental challenges inspired by real space conditions.

Solar Flares and Space Weather

Solar activity can create dangerous radiation conditions and disrupt communication systems. During simulated communication blackouts, players cannot remotely control the mini rover or use the communication desk. Players must respond to warnings and protect the astronaut.

Martian Dust Storms

Dust storms reduce sunlight reaching solar panels, decreasing electrical power generation. Dust gradually accumulates on individual panels, requiring the astronaut to travel outside and clean them to restore their efficiency.

These mechanics demonstrate how environmental conditions can affect the survival of astronauts and the operation of planetary outposts.

6. NASA Data Integration

A major objective of MISSION MOHAKASH is connecting gameplay with real NASA information instead of relying entirely on fictional space data.

We incorporate three NASA resources:

NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database)

🔗 https://kauai.ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI

The game retrieves real space-weather notifications through the NASA API endpoint. It checks the previous 30 days of events, including solar flares (FLR), coronal mass ejections (CME), solar radiation storms (SEP), and geomagnetic storms (GST).

The information is summarized in child-friendly language and displayed on the mission briefing screen. This helps players understand that solar activity and space-weather hazards are real phenomena.

NASA Moon Trek

🔗 https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/

We use NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Wide Angle Camera (LRO WAC) Global Mosaic through Moon Trek's Web Map Tile Service (WMTS). Two hemisphere map tiles are downloaded, combined, and displayed on the lunar mission briefing screen.

NASA Mars Trek

🔗 https://trek.nasa.gov/mars/

We use the Viking MDIM 2.1 global colour mosaic through Mars Trek's WMTS. The downloaded hemisphere tiles are combined and displayed on the Martian mission briefing screen.

These integrations allow players to see real planetary surface maps and real space-weather information before starting their missions.

Note: All three NASA data integrations are optional. If an internet connection is unavailable, the game remains playable.

7. Scientific Foundation

Beyond live NASA data, the game's simulation mechanics are informed by real space exploration research and engineering references.

Examples include:

  • Apollo 17 and ALSEP seismic experiments for seismometer placement concepts.
  • NASA spacesuit specifications for modelling EVA endurance.
  • Water electrolysis principles for oxygen production.
  • ISS carbon dioxide removal system data for life-support modelling.
  • NASA's MOXIE experiment on the Perseverance rover for producing oxygen from the Martian atmosphere.
  • Mars Exploration Rover mission findings for dust accumulation and solar panel efficiency mechanics.
  • Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter observations for reduced solar irradiance during dust storms.
  • Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter instruments and lunar south-pole research for lunar environmental information.

These references help connect the game's resource-management mechanics with real engineering and scientific challenges.

8. Educational Benefits and Expected Impact

MISSION MOHAKASH aims to help children understand the complexity of human space exploration through interactive learning.

By playing the game, students can:

  • Understand why astronauts need oxygen, water, food, and electricity.
  • Learn about the importance of radiation protection and spacesuit life support.
  • Discover how solar panels generate electricity and how environmental conditions affect energy production.
  • Understand why resource planning is essential for long-duration missions.
  • Explore lunar and Martian geography through real NASA planetary maps.
  • Learn about solar flares, radiation events, and Martian dust storms.
  • Develop problem-solving, critical-thinking, and decision-making skills.

Our goal is to transform space science from something students simply read about into something they can experience through meaningful decisions and interactive gameplay.

9. Development Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using the following technologies:

  • Unity 6 (6000.6.5f1): Main 3D game engine, environment, physics, rendering, and gameplay development.
  • C#: Programming language for game mechanics, simulation systems, UI, and NASA data integration.
  • Universal Render Pipeline (URP): Rendering and visual effects.
  • glTFast: Runtime loading of GLB 3D models generated using Tripo3D.
  • Unity Input System: Player controls and input management.
  • Unity UI Toolkit and uGUI: User interfaces and in-game panels.
  • Unity Timeline: Introductory cinematics and landing sequences.
  • Unity AI Navigation: Navigation and interaction pathfinding.
  • UnityWebRequest: Communication with NASA services and downloading planetary map tiles.
  • Figma: Interface and design work.

AI-Assisted Development and Asset Creation

  • Claude: Coding, refactoring, development assistance, and 3D asset creation support.
  • ChatGPT: Development assistance, problem-solving, and 3D asset creation support.
  • Google Antigravity AI: Coding, implementation, and debugging assistance.
  • Kiro AI: Development, code review, and debugging assistance.
  • Tripo3D: Generating chibi-style characters, equipment, objects, and other 3D assets in GLB format.

The generated assets and code were reviewed, customized, and integrated by our team.

10. Our Vision

We believe the future of space exploration depends not only on technological advancement but also on inspiring the next generation to understand and participate in science.

With MISSION MOHAKASH, we want to create an engaging bridge between space education and interactive gaming. Our vision is to help young learners experience the responsibilities of an astronaut, understand real mission constraints, and discover the science behind humanity's journey beyond Earth.

MISSION MOHAKASH: Explore. Survive. Discover.

Developed by Team CONFUSED UNGA BUNGA for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

MISSION MOHAKASH is an independent educational project and is not an official NASA product.
